h1: The snifter and when a small glass works better than a pint
title: The Snifter and When Small Beats a Pint | Craft Beer School
desc: What a snifter does for barley wine, imperial stout and other strong beers, the right pour size and serving temperature plus when to use one.
teaser: A 10% imperial stout in a pint glass is a mistake twice over. The snifter fixes both.
standfirst: The snifter is the short, round bellied glass that most people think of as a brandy glass. For strong beers it is often the best glass in the house. It holds a small pour, lets the beer warm up and gathers aroma where your nose can find it.
sections: A snifter is a wide bowl with a narrow mouth

A snifter has a short stem or none, a wide round bowl and a mouth noticeably narrower than the bowl. Beer snifters usually hold 250 to 400 ml in total, but the pour is small, often 150 to 200 ml. That leaves plenty of empty space in the bowl for aroma to collect.

The shape does two jobs. Swirling the beer in the wide bowl releases aroma compounds. The narrow mouth holds them in, so when you lift the glass your nose meets a concentrated cloud of smell rather than the room air.

Barley wines, imperial stouts, Belgian quadrupels and many barrel aged beers sit between 9 and 14% ABV. A 568 ml pint of a 12% beer holds nearly as much alcohol as two and a half pints of a 5% lager. That is not a sensible single serving.

A 150 ml pour in a snifter is closer to a glass of wine in alcohol and suits the way these beers are meant to be drunk: slowly, over half an hour or more. It also lets two or three people share a 330 ml bottle, which matters when strong craft beers in India often cost more than a main course. Our guide to why craft beer costs more explains where that price comes from.

Strong, dark beers taste muted straight from a fridge at 4 °C. Their rich malt, dried fruit, chocolate and oak notes come through best at about 12 to 15 °C. The snifter helps here. Holding the bowl in your palm warms the beer gently as you drink, so it opens up over the session.

In practice that means taking the bottle out of the fridge 20 to 30 minutes before pouring, then letting your hand do the rest. In an Indian summer you may need less time. In a cold, air conditioned room, a little more.
When a small glass works better than a pint

A snifter is the right glass when the beer is about depth rather than refreshment:

  • Strength. Anything above about 9% ABV.
  • Aroma. Barrel aged beers, smoked beers and beers with heavy spicing or vanilla.
  • Sharing. When a single bottle is split at a tasting or with friends.
  • Comparison. When you want to taste two or three beers side by side without drinking a lot.

It is the wrong glass for a lager on a hot day. A crisp 4.5% beer in a snifter warms too fast and loses the refreshing chill that makes it worth drinking.
Swirl first, then smell in short sniffs

Using a snifter well takes a minute of technique. Pour 100 to 150 ml. Swirl gently to coat the inside of the bowl. Bring it to your nose and take two or three short sniffs, then pause. Long deep sniffs tire the nose quickly, especially with beers above 10% where alcohol can sting.

Hold the glass slightly away first, then closer. Some aromas sit higher in the bowl, others nearer the beer. Then sip, let it sit on your tongue and notice how the flavour changes as the beer warms over 20 minutes. Our guide to a ten minute daily taste panel uses the same habits.
Pace strong beers and drink water

A snifter slows you down, which is part of its charm. Even so, strong beers deserve respect. Two 150 ml pours of a 12% stout add up to more alcohol than a pint of standard lager. Keep a glass of water alongside, eat something and never drive after drinking.

At a tasting, plan the order from lightest to strongest so the big beers do not flatten your palate for the subtle ones. Strong, sweet, high alcohol beers come last.
What to look for in the glass

A snifter is also a good glass for looking. Hold it against a white sheet of paper or a window and tilt it. A barley wine may run from deep amber to dark copper. An imperial stout should be close to opaque with a tan or brown head. Thin, fast moving legs on the side of the glass come from alcohol, a hint of strength before you taste.

Watch the head. Strong beers often have less foam than session beers because high alcohol works against foam stability. A small, tight collar of bubbles is normal for a 12% stout. A head that vanishes in seconds on a beer that should have one may point to a dirty glass or a flat beer. Our guide to the British pint glass covers how other shapes handle foam.
Pick up a snifter and pour less

You do not need a specialist beer snifter. A brandy balloon or a small, rounded wine glass works the same way. What matters is a bowl wider than the mouth and room to swirl.

Your first step: buy one strong beer you have not tried, such as a barley wine or an imperial stout. Pour 120 ml into a snifter or wine glass at about 12 °C. Smell it, sip it, then come back after 15 minutes and smell it again. Write down what changed.
faqs: What beers go in a snifter?
Strong, aromatic beers above about 9% ABV: barley wines, imperial stouts, Belgian quadrupels and barrel aged beers.
How much beer should I pour into a snifter?
Around 100 to 200 ml. The empty space in the bowl is what collects the aroma.
Can I use a brandy glass or wine glass instead?
Yes. Any glass with a bowl wider than its mouth and room to swirl does the same job.
At what temperature should strong beer be served?
About 12 to 15 °C for most strong dark beers. Take the bottle out of the fridge 20 to 30 minutes before you pour.
